takeaways: As stated in the video (November 2026): the Minneapolis median sale price was just under $370,000 in August (Minneapolis Area REALTORS) and Freddie Mac's 30-year average was about 7.3% on October 1.
Owning a $368,000 Minneapolis home with 20% down runs about $3,100 a month (principal and interest, taxes, insurance, maintenance) vs. a median $2,500 to rent a comparable three-bedroom house.
Comparing the money you never get back (interest, taxes, insurance, maintenance vs. rent), the real gap is closer to $400 a month, and it shrinks as rent rises and principal grows.
With 2.6% appreciation and a renter who spends the difference, the buyer was ahead about $5,000 after 5 years, $23,000 after 7 and $53,000 after 10, per the video's model.
Renting and investing the difference can win for 15 years or more if you truly invest every month, or if you'll stay less than about 5 years.

faq.q: Is it cheaper to rent or buy in Minneapolis?
faq.a: Month to month, renting a comparable house was about $400 cheaper in unrecoverable costs as of November 2026, Jason says, but buyers who stay 5 or more years generally pulled ahead in his model.

faq.q: When does renting make more sense?
faq.a: If you'll be in the Twin Cities less than about 5 years, your plans may change, a $1,700 two-bedroom apartment is all you need, or you'll truly invest the difference every month.

takeaways: On a $405,000 example home (near the August metro median, per Minnesota REALTORS), selling costs ran about $14,500 (3.6%) on the low end, $37,000 (just over 9%) in the middle and $57,500 (just over 14%) on the high end, as stated in the video.
Since August 2024, commissions are fully negotiable, buyers sign a written agreement with their agent, and offers of buyer-agent pay can't go on the MLS.
Some cities, including Minneapolis, St. Paul, Bloomington, Richfield, Maplewood and St. Louis Park, require a point-of-sale inspection; what the report finds is often the biggest surprise.
Minnesota's deed tax is 0.33% of the price, plus 0.01% in Hennepin and Ramsey counties.
Negotiate up front, order inspections early, fix small items, price right from day one and plan the move to avoid paying for two homes.

faq.q: How much does it cost to sell a house in the Twin Cities?
faq.a: On a $405,000 example, Jason's budget ran from about $14,500 to $57,500 as of November 2026, with commissions and concessions the biggest drivers.

faq.q: Who pays the deed tax in Minnesota?
faq.a: The Minnesota Attorney General's Home Seller Guide lists the deed tax as a seller cost: 0.33% of the price, plus 0.01% in Hennepin and Ramsey counties.

takeaways: As stated in the video (November 2026): the typical Twin Cities home sells for about $410,000, and Minnesota pending sales over $1 million jumped 42% in June from a year earlier before cooling.
Lakeville and Blaine: around $1 million buys big new construction (4,250 to 4,400 finished square feet), usually on smaller lots.
Prior Lake: a similar-size new build on more than half an acre in a golf community; lakefront starts around $1.5 to $2 million.

Plymouth buys location (a 1960s colonial on two-thirds of an acre near Wayzata), Lake Elmo mixes country land with newer homes, and Faribault gave the most house and land: 5,300+ square feet on 2.5 acres on Circle Lake.
Jason's own pick: Prior Lake for lakeshore, or Credit River for more land and a bigger house at about $1.2 to $1.5 million.

faq.q: What does $1 million buy in the Twin Cities suburbs?
faq.a: As of November 2026, examples in the video ranged from a 3,400-square-foot home in Lake Elmo to a 5,300-square-foot home on 2.5 lakefront acres in Faribault.

faq.q: Where would Jason buy a $1 million home?
faq.a: Prior Lake if he wanted lakeshore (about $2 million for something really nice on the water), or Credit River for more land and a bigger house.

takeaways: TomTom data cited in the video: Twin Cities drivers lost about 39 hours to rush-hour traffic last year, almost four more than the year before.
All three south-metro river crossings (Highway 169, I-35W and Cedar Avenue) had work; Cedar Avenue work runs through November 2028, and I-35W in Burnsville is expected to ease first.
I-494 adds E-ZPass lanes from Highway 169 to Highway 77 by fall 2030, a rebuild of about $750 million with a $135 million federal grant.
Highway 65 in Blaine gets four interchanges (about $195 million, through summer 2030); I-94 between Minneapolis and St. Paul won't see construction until about the end of the decade.
Jason isn't seeing prices near these corridors take a hit; buyers should drive the commute at rush hour and check when the work ends.

faq.q: Should I avoid buying a home near road construction?
faq.a: Jason says no: he isn't seeing prices near these corridors take a hit, and the work is temporary. Drive the commute at rush hour and find out when the project ends.

faq.q: When will south-metro road construction end?
faq.a: As stated in November 2026: I-35W in Burnsville should ease first, Cedar Avenue runs through November 2028 and I-494 phase two through fall 2030.

takeaways: As stated in the video (November 2026): the typical Minneapolis condo was worth about $228,000 in August, down 4.2% in a year, while single-family homes rose about 2.1%; condo prices are still about 9% below their 2021 peak.
Downtown Minneapolis condos had about 7.5 months of supply vs. about three months for the city across all home types.
Master insurance premiums have jumped almost 400% at some buildings, pushing up dues; every $262 a month in dues cuts a buyer's purchasing power by about $38,000.

Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac tightened condo rules: full reviews for buildings over 10 units, a $50,000-per-unit deductible cap and reserves rising from 10% to 15% of the budget in January. A building that fails loses regular loans for every unit.
Before buying or listing, check the building's lending status, reserve study, upcoming special assessments and master policy renewal date.

faq.q: Why are Minneapolis condo values falling?
faq.a: Jason cites three reasons as of November 2026: high supply, insurance-driven HOA dues and tighter Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac condo lending rules.

faq.q: What does Minnesota's new HOA law change?
faq.a: Mostly effective January 1: fines and late fees are capped, boards need three written bids on projects of $50,000 or more, members can't vote on deals they profit from, and boards can't punish owners for asserting their rights.
